# crocket guide v0.5

Generated from `guide/v0.5`, in the same order as the guide. The samples match the `0.5.2` release.


# Introduction

crocket is a C++ web framework in the same spirit as [Rocket](https://rocket.rs). It's not a port. Handlers are functions. Path captures and extractors are arguments. The return value is the response. You declare a route with a C++26 annotation, and `reflect_routes` discovers it. The wire layer is [h2o](https://github.com/h2o/h2o): HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and TLS.

This guide describes that model. The code samples match the [0.5.2](https://github.com/sean3z/crocket/releases/tag/0.5.2) release, which is the tree this site was checked against.

## What you write

A route is an ordinary function with one route annotation. Mounting a namespace picks up every annotated function in it. Helpers with no annotation stay helpers.

```cpp
namespace api {

[[= http::get("/hello/{name}/{age}")]]
auto hello(std::string_view name, std::uint8_t age) -> std::string {
  return std::format("Hello, {} year old named {}!", age, name);
}

}  // namespace api

crocket::build()
    .attach(Logger{})
    .mount("/", reflect_routes<^^api>())
    .launch({.listen = "0.0.0.0:8000"});
```

`/hello/Ada/36` calls `hello`. `/hello/Ada/400` does not, because 400 is not a `uint8_t`. The response is 404 `path.invalid`, and the handler never runs.

## Why reflection

Most C++ web frameworks bind routes with a runtime registration call, a macro, or a code generator. crocket uses C++26 static reflection instead. `reflect_routes<^^api>()` reads the functions, their annotations, and their parameter names at compile time.

- Nothing to register. You can't forget to add a route to a list, because there isn't a list.
- A mismatch is a compile error that names both identifiers. Reflection can see parameter names, which templates alone cannot.
- Reflection runs only in the compiler. Each route becomes a function pointer. A request does not pay for a string lookup, RTTI, or type erasure per argument.
- The same signatures and structs produce the JSON mapping, the OpenAPI document, and, for gRPC, the `.proto`.

The trade-off is the toolchain. You need a compiler with C++26 reflection. crocket is developed on GCC 16.2 with `-freflection`. See [Getting started](/guide/v0.5/getting-started/).

## Goals

These are the rules the framework is built around.

1. A handler is a function. `{id}` in the path is a parameter named `id`. `Json<T>`, `Auth`, and `State<T>` are more parameters. The return type is the response.
2. Route metadata lives on the function. You mount a namespace or a controller class, not a handwritten list.
3. Cross-cutting behavior belongs to the application. `attach` adds fairings. `manage` adds typed singletons.
4. Production behavior is built in: request ids, structured errors, deadlines, readiness, limits, ignite checks, and a drain on shutdown. Logging and metrics are there when you attach them.
5. One wire engine, h2o. Handlers never include h2o headers.

## Non-goals

crocket is not an ORM and not a plugin ABI. It does not reload application code without a restart. Reloading a TLS certificate is supported, because that is configuration. It does not discover routes by scanning a whole translation unit. It does not do reflection, string lookups, or type erasure per argument on the request path.

WebSockets, server-sent events, and streamed bodies are not built. What's planned on the way to 1.0 is tracked in [issue 37](https://github.com/sean3z/crocket/issues/37).

## Where to go next

If you want a running process as fast as possible, start with the [quickstart](/guide/v0.5/quickstart/). The [overview](/guide/v0.5/overview/) is the map of the rest of the guide. If you're coming from Node, read [Migrating from Express](/guide/v0.5/migrate-express/). If you're coming from Java, read [Migrating from Spring Boot](/guide/v0.5/migrate-spring/).


# Quickstart

A small program you can build once GCC 16.2 is on your `PATH`. The [getting started](/guide/v0.5/getting-started/) page covers the toolchain, Docker, and why the distro `g++-16` package is not enough.

## CMake

`0.5.2` is the current stable release.

```cmake
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.28)
project(hello_app CXX)

include(FetchContent)
FetchContent_Declare(crocket
  GIT_REPOSITORY https://github.com/sean3z/crocket.git
  GIT_TAG 0.5.2)
FetchContent_MakeAvailable(crocket)

add_executable(hello_app main.cpp)
target_link_libraries(hello_app PRIVATE crocket::crocket)
```

Linking `crocket::crocket` adds `-std=c++26` and `-freflection`. You don't set the standard yourself. crocket's examples and tests are not built, and h2o stays out of your headers.

## The program

```cpp
#include <crocket/crocket.hpp>

#include <string>
#include <string_view>

using namespace crocket;

namespace api {

[[= http::get("/hello/{name}")]]
auto hello(std::string_view name) -> std::string {
  return "Hello, " + std::string(name) + "!\n";
}

}  // namespace api

auto main() -> int {
  return build(Config::from_env())
      .attach(Logger{})
      .mount("/", reflect_routes<^^api>())
      .launch();
}
```

## Build and run

```sh
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=g++-16.2
cmake --build build
./build/hello_app
curl localhost:8000/hello/Ada
```

The release profile listens on `0.0.0.0:8000`. `CROCKET_PORT` changes the port. The first configure downloads h2o (about a 7 MB tarball) unless you point `FETCHCONTENT_SOURCE_DIR_H2O` at a checkout.

The binary needs GCC 16.2's `libstdc++`. If the loader says `GLIBCXX_3.4.35 not found`, point `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` at that GCC's `lib64`, or pass `-Wl,-rpath` to it.

`GET /healthz` is already there. It answers 200 `{"status":"ok"}` while the process is serving.


# Getting started

The quickstart assumes the compiler is already installed. This page is the part that usually takes the time.

## What you need

- GCC 16.2 or later, with `-freflection`. Clang is not tested.
- CMake 3.28 or later, and Ninja or Make.
- OpenSSL and zlib development headers (`libssl-dev`, `zlib1g-dev`), and `perl`, which h2o's build runs.
- Network access on the first configure, to fetch h2o. Set `FETCHCONTENT_SOURCE_DIR_H2O` to a local checkout to build offline.

There are no `install()` rules yet, so `find_package(crocket)` does not work. Use FetchContent, as the [quickstart](/guide/v0.5/quickstart/) does.

## GCC 16.2

Ubuntu 26.04's `g++-16` package is a pre-release snapshot (`16-20260322`). Its reflection bugs break a translation unit that mounts routes. The errors start with `accessing uninitialized member 'crocket::detail::Binding::kind'`.

The toolchain crocket is developed with is GCC 16.2 on Ubuntu 26.04. `./dev gcc` builds that compiler into `~/.local/gcc-16.2`. CI uses the image `ghcr.io/sean3z/crocket-toolchain:gcc-16.2`, which already has it.

## Try it without a toolchain

The hello image listens on port 8000:

```sh
docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 ghcr.io/sean3z/crocket-hello:stable
curl localhost:8000/hello/Rocketeer/42
```

That prints `Hello, 42 year old named Rocketeer!`. Pin `:0.5.2` when you deploy it. `:stable` tracks the stable release. `:latest` tracks `main`.

The same route, compiled in the browser, is on [Compiler Explorer](https://godbolt.org/z/Gdes8Kbdq) (GCC 16.2, `-std=c++26 -freflection`). That sketch is `examples/godbolt.cpp`. It has no h2o.

To work on an app inside the toolchain image:

```sh
docker run --rm -it -v "$PWD:/src" -p 8000:8000 ghcr.io/sean3z/crocket-toolchain:gcc-16.2
```

`./dev run` uses the dev profile, which listens on `127.0.0.1`. Inside a container, build the release tree and run the binary if you need `0.0.0.0`.

## Dev profile

`CROCKET_PROFILE=dev` is for your own machine. Compared with the release defaults it:

- Puts `ApiError::detail` in error bodies, including an uncaught exception's `what()`. Release never sends that.
- Writes readable log lines, colored on a terminal unless `NO_COLOR` is set.
- Prints every route at launch, and turns on `GET /__routes`.
- Uses a one-hour request deadline and a one-second drain.
- Binds `127.0.0.1` when `server.host` is empty, instead of `0.0.0.0`.

Anything other than `dev` or `release` (or unset, which means release) throws `std::invalid_argument` at startup.

The next page is the [overview](/guide/v0.5/overview/) of the handler model.


# Overview

A crocket program is a set of functions, a few calls that mount them, and whatever state and fairings you attach. This page is the map. The later chapters are the detail.

## A handler is a function

```cpp
namespace api {

[[= http::get("/hello/{name}/{age}")]]
auto hello(std::string_view name, std::uint8_t age) -> std::string {
  return std::format("Hello, {} year old named {}!", age, name);
}

auto helper(int) -> int;  // no annotation: not a route

}  // namespace api
```

`{name}` binds to the parameter named `name`. A name or type mismatch is a compile error that names both identifiers. Parameters that are not in the path are extractors. An unknown parameter type does not compile. The return type has to be a responder, or an awaitable of one (`Task<T>`).

One route annotation per function. Two verbs are two functions. Handlers are not templates, because reflection needs concrete parameter types.

## Mounting

```cpp
return crocket::build(Config::from_env())
    .attach(Logger{})
    .mount("/", reflect_routes<^^api>())
    .launch();
```

`reflect_routes<^^api>()` reads every annotated function in that namespace or class. The string you pass to `mount` is the URL prefix for HTTP routes. Routes are compiled at ignite into a tree keyed by path segment, so finding candidates takes the same time with 10 routes or 1,000, and the lookup allocates nothing. A route may have up to 64 segments and 16 captures.

A class can be a route scope too. Static members are ordinary handlers. Non-static members run on the instance you `manage`, and ignite checks that you did.

```cpp
class Info {
 public:
  explicit Info(std::string version) : version_(std::move(version)) {}

  [[= http::get("/version")]]
  auto version() const -> std::string { return version_; }

 private:
  std::string version_;
};

app.manage(Info{"1.4.2"}).mount("/", reflect_routes<^^Info>());
```

## If you know Rocket

| Rocket | crocket |
|---|---|
| `#[get("/hello/<name>/<age>")]` | `[[= http::get("/hello/{name}/{age}")]]` |
| `routes![a, b, c]` | `reflect_routes<^^api>()` |
| `rocket::build().mount("/", ...)` | `crocket::build().mount("/", ...)` |
| `FromParam` | `crocket::FromParam<T>` |
| Request guards | Extractors, `crocket::FromRequest<T>` |
| `Json<T>` | `Json<T>` |
| Query / `FromForm` for queries | `Query<T>` |
| `Responder` | `crocket::Responder<T>` |
| `Option`, `Result`, `status::Created` | `std::optional`, `std::expected`, `Created<T>` |
| `.manage(x)` and `&State<T>` | `.manage(x)` and `State<T>` |
| Fairings | Fairings, same hook names, as plain structs |
| `async fn` | Handlers that return `Task<T>` |
| `rocket::local::blocking::Client` | `LocalClient` |

Four things crocket adds that Rocket has no direct equivalent for: controllers, OpenAPI generated from the handlers, unary gRPC whose messages are plain structs, and a production kit (request ids, structured logs, Prometheus metrics, `/healthz` and `/readyz`, deadlines, resource pools).

HTML form bodies and multipart uploads are not a separate `FromForm` type. Query strings are `Query<T>`.

## Where a handler runs

Network I/O runs on one event loop per physical core. Hyperthreads of a core don't get a loop each. A plain function starts on a worker thread, so it may block. A handler that returns `Task<T>` runs on the event loop and must not block.

Adaptive placement is on by default. A plain route moves onto the event loops after 1,000 runs in a row under 100 microseconds, and back to workers when it turns out to block there (one run over 50 ms, or 8 over 1 ms within a second). `CROCKET_ADAPTIVE_PLACEMENT=false` keeps plain functions on workers.

## When things fail

- At compile time, when the types say so: a capture with no matching parameter, an unknown extractor, a return type that is not a responder.
- At ignite, before the server accepts a connection: unmanaged state, two routes with the same method, shape, and rank, a fairing that calls `ig.fail`, a bad proxy list.
- At `launch`, TLS certificate and key files must exist and be readable.
- On the request, when a value doesn't fit: 404 `path.invalid`, 422 from JSON or query, 401 from auth. The handler does not run.

Every problem ignite can see is reported at once, not just the first.


# Requests

A route runs only when the method, the path, and every extractor succeed. This chapter is that matching.

## Routes and captures

```cpp
[[= http::get("/hello/{name}/{age}")]]
auto hello(std::string_view name, std::uint8_t age) -> std::string {
  return std::format("Hello, {} year old named {}!", age, name);
}
```

Each `{capture}` binds to the parameter with the same name. The parameter's type decides whether the segment is acceptable. Built-in path types are `std::string_view`, `std::string`, `bool`, the integer types (range-checked), and the floating-point types. A floating-point capture has to be finite: `nan` and `inf` don't match.

Paths are split on `/` before they are decoded, so a capture can hold any character. `/hello/a%2Fb/36` calls `hello` with `name` equal to `a/b`. Dot segments are removed first and never climb above `/`. A path that decodes to a NUL byte is 400.

A capture that doesn't match a parameter is a compile error:

```text
error: static assertion failed: crocket: handler bad::hello [GET /hello/{name}/{age}]:
  path capture '{age}' has no parameter named 'age'; did you mean parameter 'years'?
```

Add your own path type by specializing `FromParam`. `parse` returns `std::nullopt` when the segment doesn't match, and the route is forwarded.

```cpp
struct Hex { std::uint32_t value; };

template <>
struct crocket::FromParam<Hex> {
  static auto parse(std::string_view s) -> std::optional<Hex> {
    std::uint32_t v{};
    auto [p, ec] = std::from_chars(s.data(), s.data() + s.size(), v, 16);
    if (s.empty() || ec != std::errc{} || p != s.data() + s.size()) return std::nullopt;
    return Hex{v};
  }
};
```

## Forwarding and ranks

A path that fails to parse doesn't stop routing. The request is forwarded to the next candidate. Candidates are tried in this order: lower `rank` first, then literal segments before captures, then mount order. If every candidate forwards, the response is 404 `path.invalid`.

```cpp
[[= http::get("/user/{id}", {.rank = 1})]]
auto user_by_id(std::uint64_t id) -> std::string;

[[= http::get("/user/{name}", {.rank = 2})]]
auto user_by_name(std::string_view name) -> std::string;
```

`/user/42` hits the first. `/user/ada` doesn't parse as an integer, so it hits the second. Two routes with the same method, path shape, and rank fail at ignite, with both handlers named.

## Methods

The annotations are `http::get`, `head`, `post`, `put`, `patch`, `del`, and `options`.

HEAD falls back to the GET route and drops the body. A method that doesn't match a path that does exist gets 405 with an `Allow` header.

## Extractors

Every parameter that isn't a path capture is an extractor. Extractors run before the handler. If one fails, its `ApiError` is the response.

| Extractor | Gives you | Fails with |
|---|---|---|
| `Json<T>` | Body decoded into `T` | 415, or 422 `json.invalid` and the other `json.*` codes |
| `Query<T>` | Query string mapped onto `T` | 422 `query.invalid` |
| `Header<"name", T>` | That header, parsed as `T` | 400 `header.missing` or `header.invalid` |
| `Auth<>` / `Auth<T>` | A verified bearer token | 401, or 403 `auth.forbidden` |
| `State<T>` | The managed `T` | Checked at ignite, not per request |
| `Deadline` | A deadline and a `std::stop_token` | Never |
| `RequestId` | The request's id | Never |
| `Client` | Address and scheme | Never |
| `const Request&` / `Response&` | The raw objects | Never |

A custom guard is a `FromRequest` specialization. A parameter type that is neither a path type nor an extractor is a compile error. So is a handler with two body-consuming extractors.

Failures are counted per route and extractor kind in `crocket_extractor_failures_total{route,kind}` when metrics are attached.

## JSON

Any plain aggregate works as JSON. No annotations are required.

```cpp
struct User {
  [[= json::from_path]] std::optional<int> id;
  std::string email;                // required
  std::optional<std::string> name;  // may be absent or null
  int age = 0;                      // may be absent: keeps its default
};

[[= http::post("/users")]]
auto create(Json<User> body) -> Json<User> {
  body->id = 1;
  return body;
}
```

By default, JSON names are the member names. A member is required unless it is `optional` or has a default. Unknown fields are ignored. Empty optionals are written as `null`. `Json<T>` reads the body straight into `T`, with no document tree in between.

Reading is strict. UTF-8 is checked. Duplicate keys are 422 `json.duplicate_key`, including keys a struct ignores. Nesting is limited to 64, strings to 1 MiB, object members to 1024, and array elements to 100,000. An integer that doesn't fit the member's type is an error, not a rounded number. `std::uint64_t` keeps all 64 bits.

Annotations change the defaults when you need them: `json::rename`, `json::rename_all`, `json::deny_unknown_fields`, `json::omit_null`, `json::as_string`, `json::unix_seconds`, `json::unix_millis`, and `json::tag` for a variant. Validation annotations (`json::email`, `json::min`, `json::max`, `json::min_len`, `json::max_len`, `json::pattern`) collect every failure into one 422 `json.validation`. `json::pattern` is compiled with the program, matches in linear time, and has no backreferences or lookaround.

`[[= json::from_path]]` on a member fills it from the URL instead of the body, so one struct can serve create and update. The id is `readOnly` in OpenAPI.

Outside a handler, `json::read`, `json::from_string<T>`, `json::to_string`, and `json::parse` do the same mapping.

## Queries and headers

```cpp
struct Page { int page = 1; std::optional<std::string> q; };

[[= http::get("/search")]]
auto search(Query<Page> p) -> std::string {
  return std::format("page {} of results for {}", p->page, p->q.value_or("*"));
}

[[= http::get("/reports")]]
auto reports(Header<"x-tenant"> tenant,
             Header<"x-page-size", std::optional<int>> size) -> std::string {
  return std::format("{} {}", *tenant, size->value_or(50));
}
```

`/search?page=2&q=rust` maps onto `Page`. A required header that is missing is 400 `header.missing`. Every request header reaches the handler, over HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2.

## Authentication

JWT and OIDC are optional. Link `crocket::auth` (it also links `crocket::client`, which fetches JWKS) and manage one `auth::Jwt`. `#include <crocket/auth.hpp>` is not pulled in by `crocket.hpp`.

```cpp
[[= http::get("/admin"), = auth::require("admin")]]
auto admin() -> std::string { return "admin\n"; }

return build(Config::from_env())
    .manage(auth::Jwt::from_env())
    .mount("/", reflect_routes<^^api>())
    .launch();
```

`Auth<>` is the untyped principal: `subject` and `scopes`. `Auth<T>` also fills `T` from the payload the way `Json<T>` reads a body. A missing or invalid token is 401. A valid token without the required role is 403 `auth.forbidden`. `auth::require` means every role. `auth::any_of` means one of them.

The default algorithms are RS256, ES256, and EdDSA. `none` is rejected. HS256, HS384, and HS512 stay off unless you set `CROCKET_AUTH_SECRET` and include the algorithm. `Jwt::from_env` adds HS256 when the secret is set. An HMAC key is only that secret. A JWK is never used as an HMAC key.

`/readyz` stays not ready until the first JWKS document has loaded. A later failed refresh keeps the keys already in memory. There is no introspection, so a token revoked at the issuer stays accepted until it expires. Verified tokens are cached on each worker until `exp` (1,024 entries).

`CROCKET_AUTH=ON` fails configure when the client is off. With both options left on `AUTO`, turning the client off turns auth off.


# Responses

The return type is the response. crocket maps a fixed set of types. Anything else is a compile error unless you specialize `Responder`.

## Return types

| You return | The client gets |
|---|---|
| `std::string`, `std::string_view`, `const char*` | 200, `text/plain; charset=utf-8` |
| A plain struct, `Json<T>`, `std::vector<T>` | 200, `application/json` |
| `std::optional<T>` | 200, or 404 when it is empty |
| `std::expected<T, ApiError>` (`Result<T>`) | The value, or that error |
| `Created<T>` | 201, with `Location` when you set one |
| `NoContent` | 204, empty body |
| `Cacheable<T>` | The payload, plus validators and optional ranges |
| `Task<T>` | Whatever `T` is, after the task finishes |
| `Response` | Exactly what you built |

```cpp
[[= http::post("/heroes")]]
auto create(Db& db, Json<Hero> body) -> Created<Hero> {
  auto hero = db.insert(*body);
  return {hero, "/heroes/" + std::to_string(hero.id)};
}
```

An empty `optional` is a 404. You don't write the status yourself. `Status<T>` sets a status code on a successful payload when none of the wrappers fit.

## Errors

Error bodies are RFC 9457 problem details (`application/problem+json`): `title`, `status`, `detail`, `code`, `request_id`, and `errors` when a validation failure has per-field notes.

```json
{"title":"Unprocessable Content","status":422,
 "detail":"field '/email': must be an email address",
 "code":"json.validation","request_id":"5f0c"}
```

Codes are stable and dotted: `path.invalid`, `query.invalid`, `json.invalid`, `auth.expired`, `body.too_large`. An uncaught exception is 500 `internal`. Its `what()` never reaches the client, except in the dev profile, where `ApiError::detail` is included.

Return `std::unexpected(ApiError::bad_request("hello.name", "name is required"))` when the handler wants a specific code. The status, the message, and the code are the whole error.

## Caching and ranges

Every 200 answer to GET or HEAD carries an ETag, a hash of the body, unless the handler set its own. Bodies longer than `limits.etag_max_bytes` (1 MiB) get no automatic ETag. Hashing is about a microsecond per 10 KiB. A client that sends the tag back in `If-None-Match` gets 304 with no body.

Wrap the payload in `Cacheable` for the rest:

```cpp
[[= http::get("/reports/{id}")]]
auto report(std::uint64_t id, State<Store> store) -> Cacheable<std::string> {
  auto r = store->find(id);
  return {r.contents, {.last_modified = r.updated_at, .ranges = true}};
}
```

`last_modified` is sent as `Last-Modified` and answers `If-Modified-Since`. When the client sends `If-None-Match`, that decides instead. `ranges = true` serves one byte range as 206. A range past the end is 416 `range.unsatisfiable`. Several ranges in one request get the whole body.

## Static files

`.mount(prefix, files{...})` serves a directory, or bytes embedded with `#embed`, under that URL prefix. Routes match before files, whichever you mount first, so a handler never waits on the filesystem. A miss is the ordinary 404. That is how `/` can serve a frontend next to an API without swallowing `/healthz`.


A directory on disk is the shortest version. `root` is opened once at ignite, and every request reads relative to it:

```cpp
.mount("/", files{
    .root = "public",
    .precompressed = true,
    .cache = {{"*.html", "no-cache"},
              {"assets/*", "public, max-age=31536000, immutable"}}})
```

`precompressed` serves a sibling `app.js.br` or `app.js.gz` when the client accepts it, so you compress once at build time. Edits to a file show up without a restart.

Embedding puts the frontend inside the binary instead, so there's nothing to copy next to it when you ship:

```cpp
static constexpr unsigned char index_html[] = {
#embed "web/index.html"
};

.mount("/", files{
    .assets = {asset("index.html", index_html)},
    .cache = {{"*.html", "no-cache"}},
    .headers = {{"*.html", {{"content-security-policy",
                             "default-src 'self'"}}}}})
```

`asset()` points at the array. A string literal's trailing NUL would be part of the file, so embed the file rather than quoting it. Only GET and HEAD read files.

A few fields you'll use immediately:

- `index` defaults to `index.html`. A directory URL that ends in `/` serves it. Without the slash the response is 308 to the path with a slash.
- `*` in a cache or header glob matches any run of characters except `/`. `*.html` matches `index.html` and not `dir/index.html`. The first matching rule wins.
- `.headers` replaces a header Shield would have set, for files that match the glob. Shield's default content security policy is `default-src 'none'`, which blocks a page from loading its own scripts and styles. Set a policy the page can live with.
- Dotfiles are hidden unless `.dotfiles` is set. A symlink is followed only when the target stays inside the root. `%2e%2e%2f` is a miss.
- `max_bytes` defaults to 32 MiB. A larger file on disk is 500 `static.too_large`. A larger embedded asset fails ignite.
- `.spa` serves the index for a GET or HEAD that missed and whose last segment has no dot. A missing `app.js` stays a 404. Routes, including `/healthz`, still win.

Embedded files send a strong ETag and no `Last-Modified`. Disk files send an ETag of size and mtime, and `Last-Modified`. `If-None-Match` and `If-Modified-Since` answer 304. One `Range` is 206. `HEAD` never sends a body.

h2o's own file handler is not used. It can't serve embedded bytes, and that code stays out of the binary.


# State

`manage` a value once. Ask for it with `State<T>` on any route. The same mechanism holds a database pool and an outbound HTTP client.

## Managed state

A route that needs state nobody manages fails at ignite, before the server accepts a connection:

```text
ignite failed:
  - GET /items/{id} (api::item) requires State<Store>, but Store is not managed
```

Ignite also rejects conflicting routes and anything a fairing's `on_ignite` flags. Every problem is reported at once.

Managed state is destroyed in reverse `manage` order at shutdown, after requests have drained. A type with `bool ready() const` is part of `/readyz`. While it returns false, `/readyz` is 503 `not_ready`.

`State<T>` is never a request-time failure. If the program is serving, the value is there.

## Databases

`crocket::db` is the API (`Db&`, `find`, `insert`, `where`, and the rest). Each database is a backend you link. Today there is one, `crocket::pg`, Postgres on libpqxx. Another backend is not in this tree. Core crocket never includes it. You link `crocket::pg` when you want it, which needs libpqxx built with the same GCC and C++26. `CROCKET_PG=OFF` skips it. `ON` makes a missing libpqxx an error. libpqxx 7.10 and 8.x both work.

Handlers name `Db&`, never the backend. Your structs stay plain: no annotations and no base class.

```cpp
struct Hero {
  std::int64_t id;
  std::string name;
  std::string alias;
  std::optional<std::string> mentor;
};

[[= http::get("/heroes/{id}")]]
auto get(Db& db, std::int64_t id) -> std::optional<Hero> {
  return db.find<Hero>(id);  // nullopt: 404
}
```

Reflection reads the struct while compiling.

- The table is the type's name in plural snake_case. `Hero` is `heroes`. Specialize `crocket::db::table_name<Hero>` to use another name.
- The columns are the data members, by name and in declaration order. The member named `id` is the key. The database fills it in on insert.
- `std::optional<T>` reads and writes `NULL`.
- An `id` may be left out of a JSON body. `insert` never sends it. An id a client does send is ignored on insert.

`db.find`, `insert`, `update`, and `erase` build their SQL at compile time. Filters name columns with member pointers (`db.where(&Hero::mentor, "Bruce Wayne")`), so a typo does not compile. `db.sql` and `db.exec` are the escape hatches. A unique violation on insert is 409 `db.conflict`.

`db::Pool` opens `pool_size` connections (default 8) when it is constructed and throws if it cannot, so a database that is down at startup stops the process. After that, `GET /readyz` runs `select 1` and returns 503 while the check fails or while the server is draining. A handler that cannot check out a connection gets 503 `db.busy`.

A query blocks the worker running its handler. Unless you set the worker count yourself, crocket raises it to the pool size. With `CROCKET_DATABASE_POOL_SIZE=16` on a 4-core machine you get 16 workers, not 4. Idle workers sleep. Each extra thread costs about 8 MB of virtual stack, not resident memory, and no CPU while idle. The worker count is capped at 1,024. A count you set yourself is used as is, even when it is smaller than the pool.

Routes that never take `Db&` pay nothing for this. With metrics attached you get `crocket_db_seconds`, pool gauges, and `db_ms` on the log line.

`CROCKET_DATABASE_URL` is the connection string. Empty leaves libpq's `PG*` variables.

## Outbound HTTP

`crocket::client` is optional outbound HTTP on h2o's client, on one of the server's event loops. There is no second network stack and no blocking call. Every method returns `Task`. Link `crocket::client` and include `<crocket/client.hpp>`. A program that does not link it does not get the client. `CROCKET_CLIENT` is `AUTO` (build it when OpenSSL 3 is present), `ON`, or `OFF`.

```cpp
return build(Config::from_env())
    .manage(http::Client{{
        .base = base,
        .timeout = 2s,
        .pool = 64,
        .retry = retry::idempotent(3),
        .breaker = breaker::consecutive(5, 30s),
    }})
    .mount("/", reflect_routes<^^api>())
    .launch();
```

A route takes `State<http::Client>` and `co_await`s `get` or `post`. Retries and the breaker are on unless a call opts out (`{.retry = retry::none}`). Only idempotent methods are retried, plus any call that sets `Idempotency-Key`. A retry budget caps retries at 20% of recent calls, at least 3. Failures are `upstream.timeout` (504), `upstream.unavailable` (503), and `upstream.circuit_open` (503).

Two services are two clients: `.with_state<Tag>()` and `State<http::Client::For<Tag>>`. An inbound `x-request-id` is forwarded. `traceparent` is not.

`examples/client.cpp` is `crocket_client_example`. It reads `UPSTREAM_BASE` and defaults to `http://127.0.0.1:9`, which refuses connections so the routes answer 503 until you point it somewhere.


# Fairings

Fairings are structured middleware. A fairing is any movable type with one or more of the hooks below. There is no base class and no `info()` function.

## Hooks

| Hook | When | Can |
|---|---|---|
| `on_ignite(Ignite&)` | During ignite, in attach order | Inspect state, config, and routes. `ig.fail` aborts launch. |
| `on_request(Request&)` | Before routing, in attach order | Rewrite the request, or return a `Response` and stop the chain. |
| `on_response(const Request&, Response&)` | After the response exists, in reverse attach order | Rewrite the response. |
| `on_shutdown()` | After the drain, in reverse attach order | Flush and close. |

`on_request` can answer the request. Returning a `Response` stops the chain, which is how maintenance mode and CORS preflights work. `on_response` runs on every response, including the engine's 413, 503, and 504, so logs and metrics don't miss a request. The first fairing you attach sees the request first and the response last.

Fairings run concurrently on worker threads. Keep shared state thread-safe. They are short and synchronous. They don't parse request bodies.

A response timer:

```cpp
struct Timer {
  auto on_response(const Request& rq, Response& rs) -> void {
    auto us = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::microseconds>(
                  Clock::now() - rq.received)
                  .count();
    rs.headers.set("x-response-time", std::format("{} us", us));
  }
};
```

## Shield

Shield is attached by default, last, so its `on_response` runs first. It sets:

- `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`
- `X-Frame-Options: DENY`
- `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'`
- `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`
- `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000` on HTTPS, never for localhost

A header the response already carries is left alone. That is how a handler, or a static-file `.headers` rule, replaces the content security policy for HTML and leaves every other response on the default. `Shield::none()` sends nothing. Attach your own to change one field:

```cpp
app.attach(Shield{}.set("content-security-policy", "default-src 'self'")
               .remove("x-frame-options"));
```

The default policy blocks a browser page from loading its own scripts and styles. A page you serve has to set a policy it can live under. This site's HTML uses `default-src 'self'` with no inline script or style.

## CORS, logs, and metrics

`Cors` is deny-by-default. `Cors::allow_origins({...})` takes methods, headers, exposed headers, credentials, and a max age. It answers preflights itself, or 403 `cors.denied` for an origin that is not on the list. It refuses at ignite to combine credentials with `*`. Without `Cors`, no cross-origin headers are sent.

`Logger` writes one line per request: request and trace ids, method, route template (never the raw path), handler, status, error code, duration, bytes, protocol, client, user agent, and the authenticated subject. `Authorization`, `Proxy-Authorization`, and `Cookie` are removed from log lines. Field names that look like credentials are redacted, and `-` and `_` count as the same character, so `X-Api-Key` matches `api_key`.

`Metrics` serves Prometheus text at `GET /metrics`, labeled by route template. The series include `crocket_http_requests_total`, a duration histogram, in-flight requests, extractor failures, connections, worker gauges, and `crocket_build_info{version,commit,compiler,hostname}`. `crocket_saturation` (0 to 1) combines the capacity signals for an HPA or KEDA target; see [Scaling](/guide/v0.5/scaling/). Scrape each pod from one Prometheus. Two scrapers would each see half of a counter that is not shared.

`CROCKET_METRICS_LABELS` adds labels. A Kubernetes Service named `crocket` injects `CROCKET_PORT=tcp://...`, which crocket refuses to start with. Set `enableServiceLinks: false`, or name the Service something else.

## Health checks

Every app gets two built-in routes.

- `GET /healthz` answers 200 `{"status":"ok"}` while the process is serving. Use it for liveness.
- `GET /readyz` answers 200 `{"status":"ready","checks":{...}}` when every readiness check passes, and 503 `not_ready` when one fails. The checks are each managed type with `bool ready() const`, and the database pool's `select 1`. During the drain on shutdown it answers 503 `server.draining`.

Static files mounted at `/` do not swallow these. Routes match first.


# Testing

Handlers are plain functions, so you can call them directly. `LocalClient` is how you test the pipeline around them without opening a socket.

## LocalClient

`LocalClient` dispatches through fairings, routing, extractors, responders, and error mapping. It plays the role of Rocket's `local::blocking::Client`. It normalizes and routes paths the same way the server does, so an in-process test cannot pass on an input the server treats differently.

```cpp
Crocket app = make_app();
LocalClient client(app);

auto res = client.post("/users").bearer("alice").json(R"({"email":"a@example.com"})").dispatch();
assert(res.status == 201);
assert(*res.headers.get("location") == "/users/1");

auto bad = client.get("/hello/Ada/400").dispatch();
assert(bad.status == 404 && bad.error_code == "path.invalid");
```

Construction ignites the app and throws if ignite fails. `.remote("10.0.0.5")` sets the peer, which is how you test trusted proxies:

```cpp
auto r = client.get("/whoami")
             .remote("10.0.0.5")
             .header("x-forwarded-for", "203.0.113.9")
             .dispatch();
```

Only a peer in `proxy.trusted` is believed. A request from any other address keeps its own address and scheme, whatever headers it sends.

`tests/acceptance.cpp` is the larger example: routing, responders, request ids, logs, metrics, health checks, CORS, pools, the dev profile, Shield, ETags, 304s, and ranges.

## Compile failures

`tests/compile_fail/` holds programs that must not compile. Each one is checked for the expected diagnostic. That includes the `{age}` versus `years` error, which has to name both identifiers, plus unknown extractors, bad JSON annotations, and return types that are not responders. A control file in the same directory must compile.

## What else the suite covers

You don't need these to test an application. They're how crocket itself is checked, and they're the contract behind the chapters in this guide.

- `json` covers round trips, limits, duplicate keys, and validation.
- `router` checks the route tree against a linear scan, including HEAD falling back to GET.
- `static` covers directories, `#embed`, index files, dotfiles, and symlink misses.
- `tls_h2` drives real sockets with ALPN h2 and HTTP/1.1.
- `openapi` checks the generated document piece by piece.
- `grpc` checks protobuf encoding and the generated `.proto`.
- `db` runs against Postgres when `CROCKET_TEST_DATABASE_URL` is set, and is skipped otherwise.

`ctest` also runs each fuzz target's corpus and two seconds of mutations. The fuzzers cover JSON, protobuf, query strings, routes, whole requests, and HTTP/2 frames.


# Configuration

One `Config` holds the server, the limits, the timeouts, the proxy, and the profile. Optional pieces read their own groups: `auth` for `crocket::auth`, `database` for `crocket::db`. Core crocket never opens a database or fetches a JWKS on its own.

## Precedence

Settings stack, and each layer beats the one before it:

1. The built-in defaults, or the `Config` you pass to `from_env` when your program wants different ones.
2. The dev profile, when `CROCKET_PROFILE=dev`.
3. The other `CROCKET_*` environment variables.
4. Whatever you assign in code after `from_env` returns.
5. The fields you pass to `launch({...})`.

```cpp
Config cfg = Config::from_env({.server = {.port = 50051}});
cfg.timeouts.request = 10s;
return crocket::build(cfg)
    .mount("/", reflect_routes<^^api>())
    .launch({.listen = "0.0.0.0:50051"});
```

`from_env`'s argument replaces the built-in defaults, and the environment can still override it. That is how a gRPC server defaults to port 50051 without ignoring `CROCKET_PORT`. `launch()` with no argument serves on `cfg.server`. `.listen` takes `"8080"`, `":8080"`, `"0.0.0.0:8080"`, or `"[::1]:8080"`.

A value that does not parse throws `std::invalid_argument` naming the variable, so a typo stops the program at startup. Sizes take `K`, `M`, or `G` (powers of 1024). Durations take `ms`, `s`, `m`, or `h`, and a bare number is seconds. Booleans are `true`/`false`, `1`/`0`, `yes`/`no`, or `on`/`off`. Lists are comma-separated. Unset or empty leaves the setting alone.

## Limits

Every resource a client can make the server hold has a bound. Past it, the request fails or the connection waits, as the table says. The defaults follow h2o for connections and HTTP/2, and Rocket for a JSON body.

| Limit | Default | Past it |
|---|---|---|
| `max_connections` | 1024 | New connections wait in the accept queue |
| `max_connections_per_ip` | 0 (none) | A new connection from that address is closed |
| `http2_max_streams` | 100 | Advertised in the HTTP/2 SETTINGS |
| `max_header_bytes`, `max_header_count` | 8 KiB, 100 | 431 `headers.too_large` |
| `max_body_bytes` | 1 MiB | 413 `body.too_large` |
| `max_body_memory` | 256 MiB | 503 `server.busy` |
| `etag_max_bytes` | 1 MiB | No automatic ETag |
| `max_in_flight` | 1024 | 503 `server.busy` |
| `timeouts.request` | 30 s | 504 `deadline.exceeded` |
| `timeouts.drain` | 10 s | In-flight requests are dropped after this |

`max_connections_per_ip` is off by default because, behind a load balancer, every connection comes from the balancer. Set it when clients connect directly. h2o also closes a connection that takes more than 10 seconds to send its headers, or that sits idle on HTTP/2 for 10 seconds (GOAWAY).

## Dev profile

`CROCKET_PROFILE=dev` selects `Config::dev()`. Unset or `release` uses the release defaults. The dev profile binds `127.0.0.1` when the host is empty, prints every route, turns on `GET /__routes`, puts error detail in the body, uses a one-hour deadline, and drains in one second. Its logs are readable lines. Release logs are structured. `allowed_hosts` in the dev profile also accepts `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, and `::1`.

## Behind a proxy

`Client` reports the peer address and whether the connection was `https` or `http`. Behind a proxy, list the proxies you run. crocket then takes both from the header they add.

```cpp
Config cfg;
cfg.proxy.trusted = {"10.0.0.0/8"};
cfg.proxy.header = ProxyHeader::XForwardedFor;  // the default
cfg.proxy.allowed_hosts = {"api.example.com", "*.example.com"};
```

Only trusted proxies are believed. Behind a chain, the client is the first address that no trusted proxy is behind, so a value the client wrote into `X-Forwarded-For` itself is never picked. Only the configured header is read. The other is ignored.

`allowed_hosts` is the host names the server answers. Any other `Host` (`:authority` on HTTP/2) is 400 `host.invalid` before routing. Ports are not compared. `*.example.com` matches subdomains and not `example.com` itself. An empty list allows every host. A malformed entry fails ignite.

`CROCKET_TRUSTED_PROXIES`, `CROCKET_PROXY_HEADER` (`x-forwarded-for` or `forwarded`), and `CROCKET_ALLOWED_HOSTS` set the same fields.

## Environment variables

The names you set most often:

| Variable | Default |
|---|---|
| `CROCKET_PROFILE` | `release` |
| `CROCKET_PORT` | `8000` |
| `CROCKET_HOST` | `0.0.0.0` (`127.0.0.1` in dev) |
| `CROCKET_LISTEN` | unset. Replaces host and port |
| `CROCKET_TLS_CERT`, `CROCKET_TLS_KEY` | unset. TLS needs both |
| `CROCKET_HTTP2` | `true` |
| `CROCKET_H2_PRIOR_KNOWLEDGE` | `false` |
| `CROCKET_WORKERS` | at least 4, one per core, raised to the largest blocking pool |
| `CROCKET_EVENT_LOOPS` | one per physical core |
| `CROCKET_LOG_LEVEL` | `info` (`debug` in dev) |
| `CROCKET_LOG_SAMPLE` | `1` (every successful request) |
| `CROCKET_LOG_SLOW` | `500ms` |
| `CROCKET_REQUEST_TIMEOUT` | `30s` (an hour in dev) |
| `CROCKET_DRAIN_TIMEOUT` | `10s` (`1s` in dev) |
| `CROCKET_DATABASE_URL` | unset (libpq's `PG*` variables) |
| `CROCKET_DATABASE_POOL_SIZE` | `8` |
| `CROCKET_AUTH_ISSUER`, `CROCKET_AUTH_AUDIENCE`, `CROCKET_AUTH_JWKS` | unset |
| `CROCKET_AUTH_SECRET` | unset (HMAC off) |

`CROCKET_AUTH_*` and `CROCKET_DATABASE_*` do nothing until you link `crocket::auth` or `crocket::pg` and construct the verifier or the pool from `cfg`. The limit variables (`CROCKET_MAX_BODY_BYTES` and the rest) map onto the table above, one name per field.


# OpenAPI

The handlers already say what the API is. `OpenApi` writes that down as an OpenAPI 3.1 document so you don't keep a second copy.

```cpp
app.attach(OpenApi{{.title = "Orders", .version = "1.4.0", .docs = "/docs"}});
```

`GET /openapi.json` serves the document for every HTTP route, built at ignite from the handlers. `GET /docs` is an interactive page. That page loads Swagger UI from `cdn.jsdelivr.net`. If your content security policy only allows your own origin, leave `.docs` unset and serve the JSON yourself. gRPC methods are left out. Their contract is the `.proto`. `/__routes` is left out too.

## What lands in the document

| In the handler | In the document |
|---|---|
| `{id}` and its parameter's type | A required path parameter, with the integer's range when it has one |
| `Query<T>` | One query parameter per member, required unless optional or defaulted |
| `Header<"x-tenant">` | A header parameter, required unless optional |
| `Json<T>` | A required `application/json` body, plus 415 and 422 responses |
| `Auth<>` | A bearer security requirement, and a 401 |
| `T`, `Json<T>`, `std::string`, `NoContent`, `Created<T>`, `std::optional<T>`, `Result<T>`, `Cacheable<T>`, `Task<T>` | The success response. 404 for an optional, 304 for a cacheable |
| Any failure | `default`: `application/problem+json` with the shared `Problem` schema |

Structs become schemas in `components/schemas`, following exactly what `Json<T>` reads and writes: renames, `as_string`, time formats, enums as their names, maps, recursion, untagged variants (`anyOf`), and `json::tag` variants (`oneOf` with a discriminator). Validation annotations become JSON Schema keywords (`minimum`, `maxLength`, `minItems`, `pattern`, `format: email`). `json::from_path` members are `readOnly`. A member is `required` when a request must send it. Two structs with the same name get qualified names (`billing.Order`).

Each operation uses the handler's name as `operationId` (`shop.create_order`), its scope as the tag, and a summary from the function name. `Auth` records the bearer scheme. `auth::require` and `auth::any_of` add `x-required-roles` and `x-required-roles-match` (`all` or `any`), plus a 403.

## Writing it at build time

To print the document instead of serving it:

```cpp
if (argc > 1 && argv[1] == "--openapi"sv) {
  std::cout << crocket::openapi_document(app, {.title = "Orders", .version = "1.4.0"});
  return 0;
}
```

The same function is what the fairing serves. Nothing is written twice, so the document can't drift from the signatures.


# gRPC

Unary gRPC methods are functions. Messages are plain structs, encoded as proto3 by reflection. There is no `.proto` to keep in sync and no generated code. Streaming is not supported.

## A method

```cpp
struct HelloRequest {
  std::string name;                                     // field 1
  std::optional<std::string> title;                     // field 2
  [[= proto::field(4)]] std::vector<std::string> tags;  // field 4 (3 was retired)
};
struct HelloReply { std::string message; };

namespace greeter {

[[= grpc::rpc]]
auto say_hello(HelloRequest req, Auth<> auth) -> Result<HelloReply> {
  if (req.name.empty())
    return std::unexpected(ApiError::bad_request("hello.name", "name is required"));
  return HelloReply{"Hello, " + req.name};
}

}  // namespace greeter

crocket::build()
    .mount("helloworld", reflect_routes<^^greeter>(), Mode::Grpc)
    .mount("/api", reflect_routes<^^api>())
    .launch({.port = 50051, .h2_prior_knowledge = true});
```

`Mode::Grpc` makes the first argument of `mount` a protobuf package (`"helloworld"`, `"acme.v1"`, or `""`) instead of a URL prefix. The service is the namespace or class and the method is the function, both in PascalCase. `greeter::say_hello` is `POST /helloworld.Greeter/SayHello`. Mounting gRPC methods without `Mode::Grpc`, or HTTP routes with it, fails ignite.

Field numbers follow declaration order from 1. `[[= proto::field(n)]]` pins a member, and the members after it continue from `n + 1`. Duplicate or reserved numbers are compile errors. Pin numbers before you reorder or remove members, because renumbering breaks existing clients.

The types are `bool`, `intN_t`, `uintN_t`, `float`, `double`, `std::string`, `proto::Bytes`, enums, nested structs, and `std::optional`, `std::vector`, and `std::map` of those. Unknown fields are skipped when decoding.

A method takes at most one request message. None means `google.protobuf.Empty`. It can also take any extractor that does not read the body: `Auth<>`, `State<T>`, `Deadline`, `Header<...>`. Custom metadata arrives as request headers, so `Header<"x-tenant">` reads it.

You can return a message, `Result<T>`, `std::optional<T>` (empty is `NOT_FOUND`), `void` (`Empty`), or a `Task` of one of those.

## Errors and deadlines

An `ApiError` becomes a gRPC status derived from its HTTP status: 401 `UNAUTHENTICATED`, 404 `NOT_FOUND`, 422 `INVALID_ARGUMENT`, 504 `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED`, and so on. `message` goes in `grpc-message`. The dotted code goes in a `crocket-error-code` trailer. `grpc::error(grpc::Code::AlreadyExists, "user.exists", "...")` picks the code exactly. An unknown method is `UNIMPLEMENTED`.

A `grpc-timeout` header can shorten `timeouts.request`. It cannot extend it.

## HTTP/2

gRPC needs HTTP/2. Over TLS it is negotiated with ALPN. A gRPC client on an insecure channel speaks h2 without TLS, which `h2_prior_knowledge` serves. The same port keeps serving HTTP/1.1. `CROCKET_H2_PRIOR_KNOWLEDGE=true` sets the flag without a code change. `examples/grpc.cpp` turns it on when no TLS certificate is configured, and defaults the port to 50051 through `Config::from_env`.

## The .proto

Other languages still want a schema. It comes from the same declarations:

```cpp
std::fputs(grpc::proto_file<^^greeter>("helloworld").c_str(), stdout);
```

That prints a `service Greeter` block and every message and enum the methods use. Enum values get their enum's prefix, as proto3 requires (`Mood::grumpy` is `MOOD_GRUMPY`). A missing zero value is added as `<ENUM>_UNSPECIFIED`. `crocket_grpc --proto` prints the schema for `examples/grpc.cpp`.

To test without sockets, `LocalClient::grpc` sends one framed message and `grpc::read_reply<T>` decodes the answer.

```cpp
auto res = client.grpc("/helloworld.Greeter/SayHello",
                       proto::encode(HelloRequest{.name = "Ada"}))
               .dispatch();
assert(grpc::read_reply<HelloReply>(res)->message == "Hello, Ada");
```


# Deploying

The release profile listens on `0.0.0.0:8000`. Put a proxy in front of it for TLS if you don't want crocket to terminate TLS itself. `launch({.tls_cert = ..., .tls_key = ...})` or `CROCKET_TLS_CERT` and `CROCKET_TLS_KEY` turn on HTTPS, and HTTP/2 is negotiated with ALPN when `server.http2` is true (the default).

On SIGINT or SIGTERM, crocket stops accepting, drains in-flight requests for `timeouts.drain` (10 seconds unless you change it), runs `on_shutdown`, and then destroys managed state. With TLS on, it reloads the certificate and key on SIGHUP and when either file changes and then stays the same for a second. A certificate that does not load, or does not match its key, is logged and the previous one stays in use.

## Docker

Published images:

- `ghcr.io/sean3z/crocket-hello`, tagged `:0.5.2`, `:0.5`, and `:stable` for the stable release, and `:latest` for `main`. Pin `:0.5.2` in anything you deploy. The tags are signed with Sigstore.
- `ghcr.io/sean3z/crocket-toolchain:gcc-16.2`, Ubuntu 26.04 with GCC 16.2. `:gcc-16.2-pg` adds libpqxx built with that GCC.

A Dockerfile for the [quickstart](/guide/v0.5/quickstart/) app, in the toolchain image so GCC 16.2's `libstdc++` is there at run time:

```dockerfile
FROM ghcr.io/sean3z/crocket-toolchain:gcc-16.2
COPY . /src
WORKDIR /src
RUN cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
      -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=/opt/gcc-16.2/bin/gcc-16.2 \
      -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=/opt/gcc-16.2/bin/g++-16.2 \
      -DCMAKE_EXE_LINKER_FLAGS="-Wl,-rpath,$(dirname $(/opt/gcc-16.2/bin/g++-16.2 -print-file-name=libstdc++.so))" \
 && cmake --build build \
 && install -m755 build/hello_app /usr/local/bin/ \
 && rm -rf /src/build
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["hello_app"]
```

Linking with `-Wl,--gc-sections` drops the parts of h2o a program never calls, about 300 KB. h2o is linked statically. OpenSSL stays dynamic, under the Apache License 2.0. A binary you distribute has to include h2o's notices and the notices of the libraries it bundles (picotls, quicly, picohttpparser, hiredis, libyrmcds, libgkc, and cloexec).

## Kubernetes

Use `/healthz` for liveness and `/readyz` for readiness. `/readyz` turns 503 as soon as the drain starts, and while a managed pool or the database is down.

Set `CROCKET_EVENT_LOOPS` to the CPU limit. crocket counts the CPUs in its affinity mask, which a CPU quota doesn't change. A `preStop` sleep keeps the pod serving until the Service has stopped sending it new connections. Keep `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` above that sleep, plus the drain, plus your slowest request.

A Service named `crocket` makes Kubernetes inject `CROCKET_PORT=tcp://...`, which crocket refuses to start with. Set `enableServiceLinks: false`, or name the Service something else.

The hello image does not attach `Metrics`. Your app does, if you want `/metrics`. Scrape each pod directly. Two scrapers would each see half of the counters. How to read `crocket_saturation`, and when more pods won't help, is in [Scaling](/guide/v0.5/scaling/).

## The wire engine

The framework layer knows nothing about sockets. `Crocket::handle` is the whole contract, and `LocalClient` drives that function. `src/engine_h2o.cpp` is the only translation unit that includes `<h2o.h>`. h2o is linked `PRIVATE`, built as `libh2o-evloop` with mruby, brotli, zstd, io_uring, and the shared library off.

Network I/O runs on one event loop per physical core in the process's affinity mask. On a 16-core, 32-thread machine, 16 loops served about 1.6 times the requests of 32, because two loops sharing a core compete for it. Each loop has its own listening socket. The sockets share the port through `SO_REUSEPORT`. A connection stays on one loop for its whole life.

Plain handlers run on a worker pool (`max(4, cores)` unless you set it, or unless a blocking pool is larger). Workers never touch an `h2o_req_t`. A `Task` runs on the loop. A completion whose request is already gone, because the client disconnected or the deadline already produced a 504, is dropped.

h2o is pinned to a master commit in `cmake/h2o.cmake`, because it has had no release tag since 2.2.6 (2019). The pin this guide was checked against is `8c95f068` (2026-10-24).

## Versions

crocket uses semantic versioning. While it is on 0.x, a minor bump may break the API, and patch releases are fixes and additions only. 1.0 is not released. There is no compatibility shim. For each minor you cross, read that version's changelog and rebuild.

| Channel | Git ref | For |
|---|---|---|
| stable | the latest `X.Y.Z` tag, now `0.5.2` | Everyone |
| latest | `main` | Trying what's next |
| experimental | `X.Y.Z-rc.N` | Testing risky changes |

The version is in `<crocket/version.hpp>`: `crocket::version::string` (`"0.5.2"`), and `commit` from git at configure time or from `-DCROCKET_GIT_COMMIT`.

The release notes are the [changelog](https://github.com/sean3z/crocket/blob/0.5.2/CHANGELOG.md). What's planned on the way to 1.0, including features not in crocket yet, is [issue 37](https://github.com/sean3z/crocket/issues/37).


# Scaling

`crocket_saturation` is one 0..1 gauge that says how close this instance is to its ceiling. Point an HPA or KEDA at it. Attach the `Metrics` fairing to serve it at `GET /metrics`.

## When to scale

| What you see | What it means | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `crocket_saturation` is steady and well under 0.7 | There is still headroom | No need to scale |
| `crocket_saturation` near or above 0.7, driven by `crocket_worker_busy_ratio` approaching 1 or mean `crocket_request_queue_wait_seconds` approaching 25 ms | Workers are full | Add pods |
| Mean `crocket_event_loop_lag_seconds` approaching 50 ms, on an app that runs only on the loops | The loops are late | Add pods, and check for CPU throttling |
| `crocket_saturation` at 1.0 from the pool input (in use / `crocket_db_pool_size` = 1.0), with `crocket_db_pool_wait_seconds` rising and database CPU near its limit | More pods will not help | Scale the database |
| `crocket_requests_shed_total` or `crocket_requests_abandoned_total` increasing, or 504s in `crocket_http_requests_total` | You scaled too late | You scaled too late |

## What it measures

It is the largest of:

| Input | Counts as 1.0 at |
| --- | --- |
| `crocket_worker_busy_ratio` | every worker busy for the whole window |
| database pool connections in use / `crocket_db_pool_size` (with `crocket::db`) | every connection checked out |
| mean `crocket_request_queue_wait_seconds` in the window / 25 ms | 25 ms average wait for a worker |
| mean `crocket_event_loop_lag_seconds` in the window / 50 ms | loops 50 ms late on average |

Each input is capped at 1. The window is the time since the previous scrape of that `/metrics`, so scrape each pod from one Prometheus. Two scrapers would each see half windows. The pool share is read at scrape time. Taking the largest input means the first resource to run out drives it. Target about 0.7, to leave headroom for spikes.

CPU percent misleads for crocket, whose time is mostly kernel I/O. `crocket_worker_busy_ratio` counts handler time directly.

Handlers crocket places on the event loop (async ones, or fast plain functions) never use a worker, so an app that runs entirely on the loops shows up in event loop lag rather than in the busy ratio.

## Autoscaling

With [prometheus-adapter](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/prometheus-adapter), expose it as a pods metric and point an HPA at it:

```yaml
# prometheus-adapter rules
rules:
  - seriesQuery: 'crocket_saturation{namespace!="",pod!=""}'
    resources: {overrides: {namespace: {resource: namespace}, pod: {resource: pod}}}
    metricsQuery: 'max_over_time(crocket_saturation{<<.LabelMatchers>>}[1m])'
---
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata: {name: heroes}
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: {apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: heroes}
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 20
  metrics:
    - type: Pods
      pods:
        metric: {name: crocket_saturation}
        target: {type: AverageValue, averageValue: "700m"}   # 0.7
```

Or with [KEDA](https://keda.sh), straight from Prometheus:

```yaml
apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: ScaledObject
metadata: {name: heroes}
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: {name: heroes}
  minReplicaCount: 2
  maxReplicaCount: 20
  triggers:
    - type: prometheus
      metadata:
        serverAddress: http://prometheus.monitoring:9090
        query: sum(avg_over_time(crocket_saturation{app="heroes"}[1m]))
        threshold: "0.7"   # per replica: KEDA divides the sum by the target
```

Useful PromQL alongside it:

```promql
# Worker busy share over 5 minutes, independent of scrape timing
sum by (pod) (rate(crocket_worker_busy_seconds_total[5m])) / sum by (pod) (crocket_workers)
# p95 wait for a worker
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(crocket_request_queue_wait_seconds_bucket[5m])))
# Already late: requests shed or abandoned per second
sum(rate(crocket_requests_shed_total[5m])) + sum(rate(crocket_requests_abandoned_total[5m]))
```


# Migrating from Express

You already know the shape: a function per route, a bit of middleware, `listen` at the bottom. crocket is that shape in C++. The handler is still a function. The arguments are the path, the query, and the JSON body. The return value is the response.

The Express examples here are Express 5.

The crocket column on this page is written against the [0.5.2](https://github.com/sean3z/crocket/releases/tag/0.5.2) release, which is the tree this site is pinned to. The same program is the [Spring Boot](/guide/v0.5/migrate-spring/) column's crocket side.

Every success response below is the same JSON. `POST /users` with `{"email":"ada@example.com","name":"Ada"}` answers 201, `Location: /users/1`, and `{"id":1,"email":"ada@example.com","name":"Ada"}`.

## Project and build

Express installs a package and starts a script. crocket is a library you compile in. You need GCC 16.2. Linking `crocket::crocket` turns on `-freflection`, so the target doesn't set the standard itself. `crocket::auth` is only there for the JWT route.

:::pair Express | crocket

```json
{
  "name": "users",
  "type": "module",
  "scripts": {
    "start": "node server.js"
  },
  "dependencies": {
    "express": "^5.1.0"
  }
}
```

```sh
npm install
npm start
```

|

```cmake
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.28)
project(users CXX)

include(FetchContent)
FetchContent_Declare(crocket
  GIT_REPOSITORY https://github.com/sean3z/crocket.git
  GIT_TAG 0.5.2)
FetchContent_MakeAvailable(crocket)

add_executable(users users.cpp)
target_link_libraries(users PRIVATE
  crocket::crocket crocket::auth)
```

```sh
cmake -S . -B build
cmake --build build
```

:::

`npm start` runs `node server.js`, the listen example below. The binary is `build/users`.

## Listen

Express binds a port when you call `listen`. crocket builds an app from `Config::from_env()` and binds it when you call `launch`. The default port is 8000. The environment can replace it, and the variable names are in the [configuration](/guide/v0.5/configuration/) chapter.

:::pair Express | crocket

```js
import express from "express";

export const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

const port = Number(process.env.PORT ?? 8080);
app.listen(port);
```

```cpp
auto main() -> int {
  return build(Config::from_env())
      .launch();
}
```

:::

`launch` serves until the process is signaled. There's no callback after listen. `GET /healthz` is already registered and answers `{"status":"ok"}`. The routes below mount onto that same builder. The program sets the port to 8080 so the rest of this page matches the Express and Spring examples.

## Path parameters

`req.params.id` is a string. In crocket the `{id}` capture has to be a parameter named `id`, and the type is checked before your function runs. `GET /users/nope` matches the route, the capture doesn't parse, and `user_by_id` doesn't run. The body is 404 `path.invalid` with detail `not found`.

:::pair Express | crocket

```js
app.get("/users/:id", (req, res) => {
  res.json({
    id: Number(req.params.id),
    email: "ada@example.com",
    name: "Ada",
  });
});
```

```cpp
[[= http::get("/users/{id}")]]
auto user_by_id(int id) -> Result<User> {
  return User{id, "ada@example.com", "Ada"};
}
```

:::

Express still runs the handler for `GET /users/nope`, and `Number("nope")` is `NaN`. crocket never calls `user_by_id` with a bad `id`.

## Query parameters

:::pair Express | crocket

```js
app.get("/search", (req, res) => {
  const page = Number(req.query.page ?? 1);
  const q = req.query.q ?? null;
  res.json({ page, q });
});
```

```cpp
struct Search {
  int page = 1;
  std::optional<std::string> q;
};

[[= http::get("/search")]]
auto search(Query<Search> query) -> Search {
  return *query;
}
```

:::

`/search?page=2&q=ada` returns `{"page":2,"q":"ada"}`. A missing query string returns `{"page":1,"q":null}`. `?page=nope` is 422 `query.invalid`, detail `query parameter 'page' is not valid`, and `search` doesn't return that struct. There's no `req.query` object to poke at.

Query values are strings. `??` only replaces `null` or `undefined`, so a missing `page` becomes `1`, and `page=nope` becomes `NaN`. `res.json` writes that as `null` with status 200. Express does not answer 422 for it.

## JSON body and validation

Express won't check the body. You do, or you add a library. crocket decodes JSON straight into the struct. `json::email` and `json::max_len` run as it decodes. A failure is 422 `json.validation`, with one problem body that lists every field.

:::pair Express | crocket

```js
app.post("/users", (req, res) => {
  const email = req.body?.email;
  const name = req.body?.name ?? null;
  if (typeof email !== "string"
      || email.length > 254
      || !email.includes("@")) {
    return res.status(422).json({
      error: "email is not valid",
    });
  }
  res.status(201)
    .location("/users/1")
    .json({ id: 1, email, name });
});
```

```cpp
struct User {
  [[= json::from_path]] std::optional<int> id;
  [[= json::email, = json::max_len(254)]]
  std::string email;
  std::optional<std::string> name;
};

[[= http::post("/users")]]
auto create(Json<User> body) -> Created<User> {
  User user = *body;
  user.id = 1;
  return {user, "/users/" + std::to_string(*user.id)};
}
```

:::

`id` is `json::from_path`. This route has no `{id}` in the path, so a body that includes `id` is 422 `json.read_only`, and the handler is what fills it in. Unknown JSON fields are ignored. Duplicate keys are an error. An empty `name` is written back as `null`. There's no schema library to keep in sync, because the struct is the schema.

crocket doesn't parse `multipart/form-data` or an HTML form body. `Query<T>` is the query string. A file upload isn't a feature you can reach for yet.

## Status codes

`Created<User>` is 201 plus a `Location` header. `Status<User>` is for the cases that don't have their own wrapper. Returning a struct with no wrapper is 200 and JSON.

:::pair Express | crocket

```js
app.post("/users/:id/archive", (req, res) => {
  const id = Number(req.params.id);
  res.json({
    id,
    email: "ada@example.com",
    name: "Ada",
  });
});
```

```cpp
[[= http::post("/users/{id}/archive")]]
auto archive(int id) -> Status<User> {
  return Status<User>{200, User{id, "ada@example.com", "Ada"}};
}
```

:::

`res.status(204).end()` is `NoContent` in crocket. You don't get a free-form status by returning a number from the handler. If none of the wrappers fit, build a `Response` yourself. The [responses](/guide/v0.5/responses/) chapter is the list.

## Middleware

`app.use` is a chain, and each layer calls `next()`. A crocket fairing is a type with a hook. There's no `next`. `on_request` runs before routing, so it doesn't know which handler matched, and it doesn't read the body. `on_response` runs after the response exists, including errors the framework produced.

:::pair Express | crocket

```js
app.use((req, res, next) => {
  res.set("x-app", "users");
  next();
});
```

```cpp
struct AppHeader {
  auto on_response(const Request&, Response& rs) -> void {
    rs.headers.set("x-app", "users");
  }
};
```

:::

Attach it with `.attach(AppHeader{})`. It runs for every request, not for one router. Route-specific logic belongs in the handler. The [fairings](/guide/v0.5/fairings/) chapter covers `on_ignite` and `on_shutdown` too.

CORS is the same idea. `.attach(Cors::allow_origins({"https://app.example.com"}))` answers the preflight or rejects the origin. There's no `cors` package to configure.

## Errors

Express error middleware is `(err, req, res, next)`, and it has to take all four arguments. A rejected promise from an async handler is passed to that middleware. crocket doesn't have that chain. Return `std::unexpected(ApiError::...)` from a `Result<T>`, or let the extractor fail. A throw the handler didn't catch is 500 `internal`, and `what()` stays out of the body unless you're on the dev profile.

`return std::unexpected(ApiError::not_found("no such user"));` is a 404 with a problem-details body. `ApiError::not_found`, `bad_request`, and `unprocessable` are the helpers. Codes are stable strings like `not_found` and `json.validation`, not whatever message you happened to send.

## Auth

Passport sessions, cookie logins, and `express-session` don't have a crocket twin. What you get is a bearer JWT. Link `crocket::auth`, manage one verifier, and mark the route. A missing or bad token is 401. A good token without the role is 403 `auth.forbidden`. Roles come from the token's `roles` claim.

:::pair Express | crocket

```js
import { auth } from "express-oauth2-jwt-bearer";

const checkJwt = auth({
  issuerBaseURL: "https://login.example.com/",
  audience: "users",
});

app.get("/admin", checkJwt, (req, res) => {
  const roles = req.auth.payload.roles ?? [];
  if (!roles.includes("admin")) {
    return res.sendStatus(403);
  }
  res.type("text")
    .send(`hello ${req.auth.payload.sub}\n`);
});
```

|

```cpp
[[= http::get("/admin"), = auth::require("admin")]]
auto admin(Auth<> who) -> std::string {
  return std::format("hello {}\n", who.subject);
}
```

```cpp
  .manage(auth::Jwt::oidc(
      "https://login.example.com/",
      "users"))
```

:::

`auth` is the `express-oauth2-jwt-bearer` package. You configure it once, and the route uses that middleware. A missing or bad token is 401 before the handler runs. The handler checks `roles` and sends 403. `req.auth.payload` is the claims, and `issuerBaseURL` discovers the keys.

`auth::Jwt::oidc` discovers the keys the same way when `jwks` is empty. A token without `admin` in `roles` is 403 `auth.forbidden`. A revoked token stays valid until `exp`. There's no introspection endpoint. `#include <crocket/auth.hpp>` isn't pulled in by `crocket.hpp`.

## Config

Express reads `process.env` wherever you like. crocket keeps one `Config`. Set the fields in code. This program only changes the port:

```cpp
Config cfg;
cfg.server.port = 8080;
```

The [configuration](/guide/v0.5/configuration/) chapter is the rest: limits, timeouts, trusted proxies, TLS. I'm not pasting environment variable names here. If you need them, they're on that page, and anything you set in code after reading the environment wins.

## Static files

`express.static` serves a directory. crocket does too, or it serves bytes you embedded with `#embed`. Routes are matched first, so a file named `healthz` can't hide `GET /healthz`.

:::pair Express | crocket

```js
app.use("/assets",
  express.static("public"));
```

```cpp
  .mount("/assets",
      files{.root = "public"});
```

:::

The [responses](/guide/v0.5/responses/) chapter has the cache and header rules.

## Logs and metrics

You'd add `pino-http` or `morgan`, and `prom-client` if you want Prometheus. Both are built in. Attach them.

```cpp
  .attach(Logger{})
  .attach(Metrics{})
```

`Logger` writes one structured line per request. The route template is in the line, not the raw path, so `/users/1` doesn't blow up the cardinality. `Authorization` and `Cookie` are dropped. `Metrics` serves Prometheus text at `GET /metrics`. It isn't StatsD and it isn't OpenTelemetry. One scraper per process. Two scrapers would each see half of a counter.

## OpenAPI

Express won't write the spec from the route table. You maintain a document, or a library reads comments. crocket writes OpenAPI 3.1 from the handlers at startup.

```cpp
  .attach(OpenApi{{
      .title = "Users",
      .version = "1.0.0"}})
```

`GET /openapi.json` is that document. `.docs = "/docs"` also serves a Swagger UI page, and that page loads its script from `cdn.jsdelivr.net`. If your content security policy only allows your own origin, leave `.docs` unset and serve the JSON yourself. This site does it that way.

## Tests

Supertest drives the Express app without a port. `LocalClient` drives crocket's real pipeline, fairings included, without a socket.

:::pair Express | crocket

```js
import request from "supertest";
import { app } from "./server.js";

const created = await request(app)
  .post("/users")
  .send({
    email: "ada@example.com",
    name: "Ada",
  });
assert.equal(created.status, 201);

const missing = await request(app)
  .get("/users/9");
assert.equal(missing.status, 404);
```

```cpp
LocalClient client(app);

auto created = client.post("/users")
    .json("{\"email\":"
          "\"ada@example.com\","
          "\"name\":\"Ada\"}")
    .dispatch();
assert(created.status == 201);

auto missing = client.get("/users/9").dispatch();
assert(missing.status == 404);
```

:::

Constructing `LocalClient` ignites the app and throws if ignite fails. Handlers are still plain functions, so you can call `user_by_id(1)` with no client at all. The [testing](/guide/v0.5/testing/) chapter has the rest.

## Docker

The image has to provide GCC 16.2's `libstdc++`, because that's what the binary was built with. The toolchain image does. The port is 8080 because `users.cpp` sets it.

:::pair Express | crocket

```dockerfile
FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY server.js .
EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

```dockerfile
FROM ghcr.io/sean3z/crocket-toolchain:gcc-16.2
COPY . /src
WORKDIR /src
ENV CC=/opt/gcc-16.2/bin/gcc-16.2 \
    CXX=/opt/gcc-16.2/bin/g++-16.2
RUN cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja \
      -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
      -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=$CC \
      -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=$CXX \
 && cmake --build build \
 && install -m755 build/users \
      /usr/local/bin/users
EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["users"]
```

:::

The [deploying](/guide/v0.5/deploying/) chapter covers TLS, the drain on SIGTERM, and `/healthz` versus `/readyz`. Use `/healthz` for liveness and `/readyz` for readiness.

## What's different

You compile. There's no reload-on-save. A wrong capture name is a compiler error, not a 404 you find in staging.

Annotations are the route table. You don't call `app.get` and hope you remembered every path. `reflect_routes<^^api>()` reads the functions while compiling.

Fairings aren't middleware. They don't call `next`, they don't see the parsed body, and `on_request` runs before the route is chosen.

There's no session store, no template engine, and no multipart parser. WebSockets, server-sent events, and streamed bodies aren't built. What's planned is [issue 37](https://github.com/sean3z/crocket/issues/37).

The memory and the throughput are measured, not guessed. [todo.crocket.dev](https://todo.crocket.dev) is a real app on this stack, not a sample pasted into a README.

## What you'd still install

crocket shows up with the boring production pieces already in the binary. Express is a fine router. The rest of this is the mall you walk through before the app feels finished.

:::parity express

`express.static` already handles files and ETags, so that row isn't a package. crocket doesn't rate-limit requests or gzip a response body, so those packages aren't in the pile either. The byte counts are published package sizes, not an installed `node_modules` and not a container image.

## By the numbers

Express isn't in this shootout. The Node column is Fastify, one process, which is the name on the homepage.

:::numbers node

:::cta
primary /guide/v0.5/quickstart/ Quickstart
/guide/v0.5/migrate-spring/ From Spring Boot
https://todo.crocket.dev Todo demo
:::


# Migrating from Spring Boot

A `@RestController` method and a crocket handler are doing the same job. The method is the route. The arguments are the path, the query, and the body. What you return is the response. crocket just refuses to discover any of that by scanning the classpath at startup. It reads the functions while it compiles.

The Spring examples here are Spring Boot 3.

The crocket column is written against the [0.5.2](https://github.com/sean3z/crocket/releases/tag/0.5.2) release. The [Express](/guide/v0.5/migrate-express/) page uses the same program. `POST /users` with `{"email":"ada@example.com","name":"Ada"}` answers 201, `Location: /users/1`, and `{"id":1,"email":"ada@example.com","name":"Ada"}` on both sides.

## Project and build

Spring Boot is a starter. crocket is a library fetched at configure time. You need GCC 16.2. `crocket::auth` is here only for the JWT route.

:::pair Spring Boot | crocket

```xml
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0">
  <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>
  <parent>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
    <version>3.5.0</version>
  </parent>
  <groupId>com.example</groupId>
  <artifactId>users</artifactId>
  <version>0.0.1-SNAPSHOT</version>
  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
      <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
      <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-validation</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
      <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
      <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-test</artifactId>
      <scope>test</scope>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
  <build>
    <plugins>
      <plugin>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
      </plugin>
    </plugins>
  </build>
</project>
```

```sh
mvn package
java -jar target/users-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar
```

|

```cmake
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.28)
project(users CXX)

include(FetchContent)
FetchContent_Declare(crocket
  GIT_REPOSITORY https://github.com/sean3z/crocket.git
  GIT_TAG 0.5.2)
FetchContent_MakeAvailable(crocket)

add_executable(users users.cpp)
target_link_libraries(users PRIVATE
  crocket::crocket crocket::auth)
```

```sh
cmake -S . -B build
cmake --build build
```

:::

The jar name follows the artifact id and version. The crocket binary is `build/users`.

## Listen

`SpringApplication.run` starts the process. crocket builds an app from `Config::from_env()` and binds it when you call `launch`. The default port is 8000. Spring Boot's default is 8080. The variable names are in the [configuration](/guide/v0.5/configuration/) chapter.

:::pair Spring Boot | crocket

```java
@SpringBootApplication
public class UsersApplication {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    SpringApplication.run(
        UsersApplication.class, args);
  }
}
```

```cpp
auto main() -> int {
  return build(Config::from_env())
      .launch();
}
```

:::

`launch` serves until the process is signaled. Tomcat isn't a separate choice. h2o is the wire engine, and your handlers never include its headers. `GET /healthz` is already there. The routes below mount onto that same builder. This program sets the port to 8080 so the rest of the page matches a Spring app on 8080.

## Path parameters

`@PathVariable` and `{id}` are the same idea. The difference is when the check happens. crocket won't call the function if `id` isn't an `int`.

:::pair Spring Boot | crocket

```java
@GetMapping("/users/{id}")
User userById(@PathVariable int id) {
  return new User(
      id, "ada@example.com", "Ada");
}
```

```cpp
[[= http::get("/users/{id}")]]
auto user_by_id(int id) -> Result<User> {
  return User{id, "ada@example.com", "Ada"};
}
```

:::

`GET /users/nope` matches the route, the capture doesn't parse, and the function doesn't run. That body is 404 `path.invalid` with detail `not found`. Spring raises `TypeMismatchException` before `userById` runs, so that case is not the method's empty body.

## Query parameters

:::pair Spring Boot | crocket

```java
public record Search(
    int page, String q) {}

@GetMapping("/search")
Search search(
    @RequestParam(defaultValue = "1")
    int page,
    @RequestParam(required = false)
    String q) {
  return new Search(page, q);
}
```

```cpp
struct Search {
  int page = 1;
  std::optional<std::string> q;
};

[[= http::get("/search")]]
auto search(Query<Search> query) -> Search {
  return *query;
}
```

:::

One struct is the whole query string. You don't repeat the names as `@RequestParam`s. `/search?page=2&q=ada` returns `{"page":2,"q":"ada"}`. A missing query string returns `{"page":1,"q":null}`. `?page=nope` is 422 `query.invalid`, detail `query parameter 'page' is not valid`, and `search` doesn't return the struct.

`defaultValue` and `required = false` are the documented `@RequestParam` attributes. A value that isn't an int raises `TypeMismatchException` before `search` runs. That is not crocket's 422.

## JSON body and validation

`@Valid` on a record is Jakarta Bean Validation. crocket's annotations sit on the members and run while the JSON is decoded. You don't register a `MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter`. The struct is the schema.

:::pair Spring Boot | crocket

```java
public record NewUser(
    @Email @NotBlank @Size(max = 254)
    String email,
    @Size(max = 80) String name) {}

@PostMapping("/users")
ResponseEntity<User> create(
    @Valid @RequestBody NewUser body) {
  var user = new User(
      1, body.email(), body.name());
  return ResponseEntity
      .created(URI.create("/users/1"))
      .body(user);
}
```

```cpp
struct User {
  [[= json::from_path]] std::optional<int> id;
```
